items.titleEn: Two Post Towns, One Short Walk
items.bodyEn: Akasaka lies only sixteen chō, about 1.7 km, beyond Goyu: the shortest gap between any two Tōkaidō post towns. Both towns lived on their inns, and their serving women competed to pull travelers in. Hiroshige's Akasaka print looks into an inn courtyard at dusk: a cycad palm, guests bathing and resting, maids dressing by lamplight before the evening meal.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Fifty-three Stations (Hōeidō ed.), Akasaka; Edo post-town records

items.bodyEn: A hatago, the inn where Edo travelers slept and ate, began as a basket. The word first meant the woven container that carried a horse's feed on a journey, then any box of travel provisions, then the meal served at a lodging, and finally the lodging itself: the inns that gave Akasaka and Goyu their livelihood.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien and Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entry 旅籠 (はたご)

items.bodyEn: In this station's 〜最中に the kanji are read さいちゅう: right in the middle of an action. Read さなか, the same word means the height of a season, as in the depth of winter. Read もなか, it is the wafer sweet filled with bean paste, named after 最中の月, the full mid-autumn moon that Edo confectioners shaped it to resemble.
items.ja: {食事|しょくじ}の{最中|さいちゅう}に
items.kana: しょくじのさいちゅうに
items.sourceNote: Daijisen, entries 最中 (さいちゅう・さなか・もなか)

items.bodyEn: Reduplicated gitaigo such as きらきら, のろのろ or どきどき are usually accented on the first mora when they work as adverbs: the pitch drops right after the first き in きらきら光る. Attach する and the same word commonly flattens to heiban, with no drop at all. The shift tells you whether the speaker is describing a manner or naming a state.
